summary:
Argentina's Gender Identity Law 26,743, promulgated on 24 May 2012 after approval in the Chamber of Deputies and in the Senate on 9 May 2012, allows adults to change legal gender, image and birth name on civil registries without surgery, hormone therapy, a psychiatric diagnosis of abnormality, or approval by a doctor or judge. The United Nations described the statute as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

On 20 July 2021, Decree 476/2021 required the national civil registry to offer a third gender marker X on all national identity cards and passports, including for non-citizen permanent residents holding Argentine identity cards. Mendoza Province and Santa Fe Province had earlier allowed applicants to leave the sex entry blank.

The same 2012 law grants adults access to sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy through public and private health care plans, with equal access stated for non-binary, transgender and gender non-conforming persons.

In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for persons under age 18. Legal experts described the measure as illegal and unconstitutional and as a setback for adolescents' rights. In April 2025 a Federal Court ruled the ban unconstitutional, restoring access nationwide.

A second February 2025 decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. The sources do not provide its operative terms.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since 1887 under Law No. 1,920. Same-sex marriage was legalized on 15 July 2010 with the same benefits and protections as opposite-sex marriage, including adoption since July 2010. A nationwide registered partnership, the union convivencial under the Civil and Commercial Code, has been available since 1 August 2015.

Penal Code Article 80(4), as amended in 2012, imposes life imprisonment for homicide motivated by hatred based on gender identity or expression and on sexual orientation. As of 2019 no national law expressly addressed discrimination or harassment based on gender identity. Outright International records that anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws. The national anti-discrimination agency was abolished and shut down in February 2024 as a public-spending measure.

The Observatorio Nacional de Crimenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a record year averaging one every 38 hours. The monitoring group described the figure as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.

In interviews in Buenos Aires on 4 April 2025, reported on 10 April 2025, trans activists including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayan and for Lohana Berkins said the policies of the Milei administration had made the community more vulnerable to violence. Sacayan, a trans activist, was killed in 2015.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of Diana Sacayan. The Court rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that a cassation court had removed in 2020, with the result that the gender-motivated-crime aggravator is currently not applied in the case.

Outright International's Argentina overview, updated 12 March 2026, notes that Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalize marriage equality and that its 2012 law allowed legal gender change without medical procedures or judicial approval. Its current assessment records negative evaluations on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration, indicating deterioration.
tangentialFactors:
Early applications of the recognition regime included a 2007 Supreme Court ruling that a 17-year-old had the legal right to undergo the sex-change process and change documents, Marcela Romero's successful legal identity change in 2009, and the 2013 official name change of six-year-old Luana, designated male at birth, reported as the first such change for a transgender child.

Trans women survivors gave court testimony in 2023 about dictatorship-era detention in clandestine centres, stating that they were hunted by the state and, once imprisoned, forced to perform sexual acts in exchange for food.

The World Health Organization in 2015 cited Argentina as an exemplary country for provision of transgender rights.
localsOnly:
For residents, the health entitlements under the Gender Identity Law operate through public and private health care plans covering surgery and hormone therapy for adults.

A 2013 law approved 204 to 1 with 10 abstentions gave lesbian couples equal access to in vitro fertilization, with filiation by procreative will under Article 562. In 2024 the Supreme Court rejected a gay couple's surrogacy claim seeking a new birth certificate omitting the surrogate woman.

Residents may also use the nationwide union convivencial in addition to marriage. Earlier local civil-union regimes in Buenos Aires city and Rio Negro Province in 2002 to 2003, Villa Carlos Paz in 2007 and Rio Cuarto in 2009 did not confer adoption rights.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in the sources is the operative content and enforcement practice of the February 2025 decree on housing of transgender people in prisons.

Not sourced beyond the ruling itself is the administrative implementation of the April 2025 Federal Court decision restoring gender-affirming care for minors nationwide.

Not sourced is whether the X marker or other registry changes are available to short-term visitors as distinct from citizens and permanent residents.

Not sourced is any transgender-specific public-attitude polling for Argentina. Attitudinal percentages in the inventory concern homosexuality and are not carried as findings about transgender persons.
